'''badinage''' (bad-i-näzh′ or bad′i-nạ̄j), ''n.'' [F., < ''badiner'', jest, make merry, < ''badin'', jesting, frivolous, < Pr. ''badar'' (= F. ''bayer''), gape, < ML. ''badare'', gape: see ''bay''<sup>4</sup>.] Light playful banter or raillery.
{{smaller block|He seems most to have indulged himself only in an elegant ''badinage''.
{{right|''Warburton.''}}}}
='''Syn.''' Raillery, banter.

'''badinerie''' (ba-dē′ne-rē), ''n.'' [F., < ''badiner'', jest: see ''badinage''.] Light or playful discourse; nonsense; badinage. [Rare.]

{{right|''Shenstone'', Works, II. 240.}}}}

'''badineur†''' (bad-i-nėr′), ''n.'' [F., < ''badiner'', jest: see ''badinage''.] One who indulges in badinage; a trifler.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To practise deceit; shuffle; quibble.
{{smaller block|Do we not palpably ''baffle'' when, in respect to God, we pretend to deny ourselves, yet, upon urgent occasion, allow him nothing?
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, I. 437.}}}}
'''2.''' To struggle ineffectually; strive in vain: as, the ship ''baffled'' with the gale.—'''3.''' In ''coal-mining'', to brush out or mix fire-damp with air, to such an extent as to render it non-explosive.

'''baffle''' (baf′l), ''n.'' [< ''baffle'', ''v.''] '''1†.''' Disgrace; affront.—'''2†.''' Defeat; discomfiture.

{{right|''South.''}}}}

'''bafflement''' (baf′l-ment), ''n.'' [< ''baffle'' + ''-ment.''] The state of being baffled, frustrated, or thwarted in one’s endeavors; want of success after repeated attempts. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Associated in his mind with ''bafflement'' and defeat.
{{right|''J. S. Blackie'', Self-Culture, p. 99.}}}}

'''baffle-plate''' (baf′l-plāt), ''n.'' A metal plate used to direct the flames and gas of a furnace to different parts of a steam-boiler, so that all portions of it will be evenly heated; a deflector.

'''baffler''' (baf′lėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who or that which baffles.

''bæftan'', ''beæftan'', ''be æftan'', < ''be'', by, + ''æftan'', aft: see ''be-''<sup>2</sup> and ''aft'', and cf. ''abaft''.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' Behind; in the rear; ''naut.'', abaft. [Archaic.]

'''II.'''† ''prep.'' Behind.

'''baft<sup>2</sup>''', '''bafta''' (baft, baf′tä), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''baftah'', ''baffeta'', ''boffeta''; < Hind. ''bāfta'', a kind of cotton cloth, ''bāft'', weaving, a web, < Pers. ''baft'', wrought, woven.]   A fine cotton fabric of Oriental manufacture; especially, a plain muslin, of which the Surat manufacture is said to be the best. {{smaller|The bafts of Dacca in British India are an inferior quality of the muslins made in that district, and are said to be manufactured from European thread. The name is also given to similar fabrics made in Great Britain. Also ''baffeta''.}}

'''bag<sup>1</sup>''' (bag), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bag'', ''bagge'', of uncertain origin, perhaps < Icel. ''baggi'', a bag, pack, bundle (cf. the older ''böggr'', a bag), appar., with assimilation, < *''balgr'', ''belgr'', skin, bellows, = Goth. ''balgs'', a wine-skin, = OHG. ''balg'', MHG. ''balc'', G. ''balg'', a skin, = D. ''balg'', skin, belly, = AS. ''bælg'', ''belg'', ''bælig'', ''belig'', a bag, > mod. E. ''belly'' and ''bellows'': see ''belly'', where other forms are given, and ''bellows''. Cf. OF. ''bague'' = Pr. ''bagua'' = It. dial. ''baga'', a bundle, baggage, ML. ''baga'', a bag, chest, baggage, belongings, appar. from the Teut. or the similar Celtic forms.]   '''1.''' A small sack; a portable receptacle or repository of leather, cloth, paper, or other flexible material, capable of being closed at the mouth; a wallet; a pouch: as, a flour-''bag''; a carpet-''bag'' or traveling-''bag''; a mail-''bag''. Specifically—'''2.''' A purse or money-bag.
{{smaller block|He was a thief, and had the ''bag''. {{right|John xii. 6.}}}}
'''3†.''' A small silken pouch in which the back hair of the wig was curled away.
{{smaller block|A bob wig and a black silken ''bag'' tied to it. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''4.''' What is contained in a bag; in ''hunting'', the animals bagged or obtained in an expedition or a day’s sport.
{{smaller block|The ''bag'' is not the sole aim of a day afield.
{{right|''Forest and Stream'', XXI. 2.}}}}
'''5.''' A sac or receptacle in animal bodies containing some fluid or other substance: as, the honey-''bag'' of a bee.—'''6.''' An udder.
{{smaller block|The cow is sacrificed to her ''bag'', the ox to his sirloin.
